utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Unfortunately, Judge Van Den Wyngaert is not able to sit today. The expectation is that she'll be able to sit again by next Monday. Under the Rules Judge Thelin and I think it is in the interests of justice to continue the hearing in her absence. She will, of course, be able to review the transcript and, if necessary, the tapes of the evidence, so that she can become familiar with what has occurred in her absence. Morning, Mr. Kypr. May I remind you of the affirmation which still applies. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning Mr. Kypr. I am about to pick up where I left off yesterday. I was asking you questioned about the interaction between the monitoring mission as a whole, especially the Belgrade regional headquarters, and the Red Cross, the International Committee of the Red Cross. We finished yesterday with Vukovar 9, tab 25, 321, Exhibit 321. So, Mr. Kypr, if you could please have that document ready. As we saw yesterday, there is no date on that document. All we have is the fax number in the upper left corner. It was probably sent sometime in December of 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This document is called "Vukovar relief mission, 20 to 22 November." Could you now please turn to page 2. There is a total of eight pages in this document. Please go to page 2. The number for the English is 00381418. Sir, can you see in the upper left corner a title which says "Team reports."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The paragraph is marked with number 7. It says that: "[In English] Two teams supported from Sarajevo were all heavily involved in the convoys and their reports are as follows." [Interpretation] Is that an accurate reading of paragraph 7, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Following that we have under (a) team Alpha and Charlie, and on the next page marked, the last four digits, 1419, we have item (b): "[Previous translation continues] ... [In English] And Sarajevo." [Interpretation] Since this is in the plural, it seems to imply that there were several teams involved. Would that be a fair assessment, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is something in the transcript, I'm talking about line 17, under item (b) it should be: "Teams Belgrade and Sarajevo." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could please go to page of this document, the last three digits of the ERN number is 432. At the top of that page we read "Conclusions." Is that, sir? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Kypr, to conclude, that the conclusions are in relation to the reports of all the teams that I have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that I am not aware what are the -- the all resources of -- for conclusions for -- for this report. So it is maybe, and I am convinced that mostly there are used as a basis or resource is -- are reports from monitoring teams, but I am not aware about the procedure in Zagreb, so I cannot say if there are other resources involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I remember you answered yesterday, but we did establish that this was a joint report, and that it was sent from the headquarters of the monitoring mission, the one in Zagreb, which comprised all the teams, the Sarajevo, Zagreb and Belgrade teams, as well as any other local teams. Let us, however, go back to our conclusions. I'm talking about item 9 at paragraph 9 in the same page. Paragraph 9 reads: "[In English] The humanitarian convoy was hampered throughout its operation by." [Interpretation] Colon. Do you agree with me that under paragraph 9 we have items (g) through (g)?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to paragraph (g), which is something that we talked about yesterday. I would like to round this off. This is something that we had interrupt yesterday. Paragraph (g) reads: "[In English] The absence of any focal point for overall control, i.e., the ICRC." [Interpretation] Sir, this is my last question in relation to this document. Do you agree with me that in this way the Zagreb-based monitoring mission or the mission as a whole, not just the Belgrade team, expressed a number of complaints to the International Committee of the Red Cross about their actions and behaviour and about the way they influenced the success of the humanitarian convoy?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this sentence or this paragraph (g) in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine, I'm happy with that kind of answer, sir. You said it yourself, after all, you can't always be able to know what somebody else meant when writing reports on behalf of the monitoring mission. You were not a member of each and every one of those teams, were you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: By that same token, you were not involved in drafting each and every one of these reports, were you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will not ask you any further questions about these ICRC documents. My learned friends will ask you more questions about this during their own cross-examination. I would like to ask you something else now, sir. Would you agree with me that to a certain degree there was competition in -- in terms of remit, and especially in terms of interests between the ECMM and the ICRC in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Our capacities were very limited, and we would be very happy if any other body is able to fulfill all possible assistance on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any conclusions as to whether all these reports and every single time the ICRC has mentioned the references that we've been through, can these perhaps provide an overall picture indicating that the ICRC did not meet the standards of success on the ground that are usually expected in situations like these?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I can, sir. Would you agree with me that after all these reports covering the various activities undertaken by the ICRC we may conclude that the ICRC did not fully meet the standards that its situation would normally have required?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you that ECMM didn't know everything about the work of International Red Cross, because International Red Cross is very independent and must be a very independent organisation. So I don't think that you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, sir, when you suggest that the International Red Cross is an independent organisation; entirely so, in fact. But I think you might agree with me that in your reports you made continuous assessments of their work, not as a matter of principle, but by judging specific situations that occurred in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know report of Colonel Cunningham, for instance, from Vukovar. But I cannot say, or I cannot confirm the word "constantly" or "continuously". And in Vukovar it was visible that International Red Cross couldn't fulfill its duty, because both, as International Red Cross representatives, as ECMM monitoring mission, we were blocked before the bridge and we couldn't go to the spot, to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We'll move on to something altogether different now. Can we please go to tab 7? The document is E5. I think 305, Exhibit 305 and 306. You agree with me, sir, that this is a report of team 6, dated the 12th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of that team at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the document that you have in front of you, is it not made up of two similar documents? Or, rather, was it written by another member of the same team that you were a part of?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Waters from United Kingdom, but I am not sure. Definitely it is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Can you please go to paragraph 4 of that document, page 3 out of a total of four pages, the ERN number in English 00381363. This is a document about the situation in Ilok and about preparations for an evacuation in Ilok; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, whoever wrote this document probably a colleague, Mr. Waters, referred to the situation, or rather to refugees from the village of Lovas, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is written that many of them were from Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Can you please go to the very last sentence of that paragraph? Or I could just read it aloud to you. "[In English] We asked for accurate number of refugees to be prepared soon." [Interpretation] Do you remember that sort of request being made by the monitors?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but it is obvious if we are -- if we have to be prepared for some event or some situation, we have to know as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you perhaps familiar with the fact that a list with this approximate figure of Lovas refugees was ever forwarded to the monitoring mission office in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that a document like this was submitted directly to the Zagreb headquarters of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was a request made to have such a list at a later stage, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, can you please confirm that you said "I don't know" in answer to the previous two questions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can we please now go to tab --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again, the answer was not recorded. The answer to my previous question. My question was: "No" -- the witness answered no to both my previous questions. He said he didn't know, or rather that he did not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand from that that you agree that your answer was no to both previous questions; is that correct, Mr. Kypr?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I -- sorry. Your Honours, I -- I answered, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to everybody, Your Honours. I am getting ahead of myself with my questions. I will try to have no further part in this confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, can we now please go to tab 13? This is document L-1. It's in relation to Lovas. 309 is the exhibit number. This document was produced on the 18th of October, or rather it was sent on the 18th of October 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The document refers to a visit made by the team to the village of Lovas, among other villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day you were with your colleague, Mr. Cunningham. You went to five different villages: Sarengrad, Opatovac, Bapska, Mohovo, and Lovas, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is missing in transcription Mohovo. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can please have a look, sir, it's midway through the report somewhere, there's a sentence that reads: "[Previous translation continues] [In English] ... stopped."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The transcript should reflect the fact that I quoted the portion of the relevant text. It says: "The team stopped." Mr. Kypr, I'll just read that sentence out to you. "[In English] The team stopped in Lovas and met with several local authorities." [Interpretation] You remember that meeting, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remember where and --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no -- my answer, yes, that I remember that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember where the meeting was held with the people from Lovas?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly it could be a school or some pub, because rooms were relatively vague, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember how many persons attended, a rough figure at least?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our side we were two. There were on the left side sitting those -- were sitting those people from local, top, let's say. And there were on -- on my right some other people. I can't say anything about them. Maybe altogether the local people were there, more than five and less than 15. I -- I have no idea, because I was concentrated on -- on the -- on the most important man.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if this man, which you describe as the most important man at that meeting, was wearing civilian clothes on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remember if he introduced himself at the meeting as the boss of the civilian authorities or the military authorities in that village?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Maybe something is written in -- in -- or my remarks or in the report, but I don't remember. But he was speaking that he was a leader of the unit which attacked the -- the city, or the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will be asking you more about that, sir. Did this person introduce himself to you in any way at all, such as first and last name, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you testified in the Dokmanovic case - for my learned friend's benefit this is 1364, that's the page reference in the relevant transcript - you stated that he was a military commander and that, in a way, he introduced himself as the mayor of that particular village. Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also not true that at the time he said to you that he had drafted a system of provisions for the village and control of the village himself?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if, at the time when you spoke to him, he told you that he had seized control of the village himself, aided by the local population, or whether there were some other forces aiding him in this?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if that leader, which seems to be how you have described him, referred in any way to a presence of the JNA in the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. If I can add, in the entrance to the village we saw the tank, but it was the tank T-34, so I am not aware if it is JNA tank or from some other unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember him perhaps telling you that he himself was a resident of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you were heard in the Dokmanovic case, this is 1365, you went on record as saying, and I think the same thing is reflected in your statement to the OTP investigators, that he told you that he had invested a lot of money in effort to get enough equipment and weapons for that group which eventually liberated that village. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect to my learned friend, would it not perhaps be better for the witness to have a short extract of what he says in relation to this incident so that he is able to either clarify or deny whether he said that or not? It's not a large extract; I've got it here before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It might be helpful, Ms. Tapuskovic, if you have one there. If not, it seems Mr. Moore --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree, Your Honours. I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is page 5 of your statement. "[In English] I also remember that he stated that the attack had been carried out by their own detachment of Serbian volunteers, that they had no need, JNA support, and that he had personally invested a huge amount of German marks for supplying the detachment." [Interpretation] Open brackets, "[In English] (Exact figure, but I cannot recall it)." [Interpretation] Mr. Kypr, do you now know what my reference is to?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that I have jogged your memory about what that person said to you, this equipment that he had paid a lot of money for, can this equipment be considered to have been weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that this person's name is Ljuban Devetak, would that mean anything to you right now?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat the person's name for the transcript. Ljuban Devetak. What if I told you that this person was not at the time residing in Lovas, this person was residing in Osijek, which is a different town in Croatia. I suppose you know where it is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Last Friday, while testifying in chief, you told us -- or, rather, that the impression he made on you was of not being an entirely sane person?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only on me, but Colonel Cunningham was very surprised.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, your report dated the 18th of October, why is there no reference in it to anything like this?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in our report you can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To cut it short, Mr. Kypr, can we read in your statement that that person told you that he had invested a certain amount of money to purchase equipment?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were sitting there for maybe one hour, and that was really a long discussion. So it is up to our evaluation what is necessary to -- to put into the -- the information to the report. The report was written by Colonel Cunningham. And I don't think that all we were told is -- is necessary to write down, because if -- if the person -- if Colonel Cunningham and me, we had some problem with this person, so then even to write everything is -- is wasting of time. And it's not usual you can see other reports that they are even short, even if we were there for the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said they spent only an hour in that conversation. You visited five villages on that day and you spent but an hour in the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... one hour, approximately one hour, because I don't remember, and I don't think that there are some time marking in our report or -- or in my remarks.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just to correct the transcript, page 13, line 10, the beginning of the answer of the witness was that he cannot claim with any certainty that the meeting lasted for one hour only. But, regardless, when you testified in the Dokmanovic case as well as here, on Friday you found it necessary to mention that the person behaved rather strangely and that he invested a substantial amount of money to purchase weapons.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember whether the other people who attended the meeting carried weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that you were present at a meeting during which an adventurer made use of the war and the entire situation in which he used all of his money and imposed himself as the village leader?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that he handed over a list to you. It is a handwritten list of names of those allegedly killed and there were 23 people, out of which 22 were Lovas residents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did either you or Mr. Cunningham in any way seek confirmation from anyone else who attended the meeting as to whether, indeed, all the people on the list were Lovas residents?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no situation to check it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion and at that meeting, or perhaps when you entered or left Lovas, did you see any other units that you could describe as paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you that in the entrance to the village there was a tank, T-34, plus some people, but I remember mostly volunteers. Because of their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to refresh your memory as to a part of your evidence in the Dokmanovic case, and I can see that you have the transcript before you. That's page 1366. Line 2 of that page, I will read it out to you. "[In English] These were the forces of the first attack. But this is a matter of what we were told, in fact, because in view of the rules under which we operated we were never in the areas where the paramilitary operations were proceeding." [Interpretation] Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I presume you can confirm to us that the visit that lasted approximately an hour was your only visit to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as concerns me or -- or Cunningham, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any other team reached the village of Lovas in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure, but I believe that there was one team of ECMM after the Ilok surrender. But I have no evidence, or I have no knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to ask you. You said that you were told at the time that the village of Lovas had about 1800 inhabitants, out of which 36 [as interpreted] were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in my testimony or in -- in this report, then -- yes, it is in report. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a clarification for the transcript. Page 15, line 12, it reads "36 Serbs," and it should be 136.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Either you or any other member of the team, did you know that out of the 1800 inhabitants of Lovas village around 180 men of the village were deployed or rather organised in six platoons to defend the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I told you that the way the village defence was organised, as well as a plan of -- of getting supplies for the village was drafted back in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot refer to that, because I have no knowledge about this situation, and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You probably didn't even know that one of those who were defending Lovas was Marin Vidic, a.k.a. Bili, and you had heard of him whilst you were out in the field?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. We were not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your role was to monitor the situation, and as monitors were you also tasked with gathering data?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, if it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were unable to do so because your visits were short? I don't know in which report exactly it is mentioned that there was a shortage of personnel and teams, but thanks to that, you were unable to collect precise information about the situation in the villages and localities you visited?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went there to observe the situation, which is there in the very moment. We are there to investigate the situation on the spot. To details means a lot of capacities, and it goes even sometimes, I believe, even beyond our mandate in details. Because we are not -- we were not allowed to -- to get information which could be seemed like that we are doing some intelligence or something like that. We have to be a trustful body, so -- so we try to be as impartial and possible visibly, and if we are doing this in detail, it belongs more to humanitarian organisations or to organisations of law enforcement, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, to go back to a document, that is this document, Lovas 1, tab 13, page 2. The final three digits of the English ERN are 395. If you have a look at tab 16, that is Ilok 12, page 2 of 2, the final figures, 380. But if you compare the pages, you can see that it's actually the one and the same page.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was told by the Prosecutor yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My learned friend, Mr. Moore, established that these were indeed the same pages, or rather that one and the same page was attached to two documents. Mr. Kypr, can you tell us whether the other document, the second document, Ilok 12, in tab 16, was this the way it was forwarded from the regional centre in Belgrade to Zagreb, comprising these two pages?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that it's my mistake during -- when I was making copies from those files, so it's -- it's my mistake, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Kypr.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Tapuskovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. [Interpretation] This team's problem is that we always come last, and we are always the ones who are forced to keep the track of time the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you do it so well, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kypr. My name is Mr. Lukic. I am an attorney appearing on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin, and I will be butting questions to you next. I would yet again kindly ask you to wait a few seconds after I have finished my question or watch the transcript, otherwise everyone participating in the proceedings will have a problem with the transcript in particular. I will begin with a question resulting from one of your answers yesterday when Mr. Vasic was putting questions to you and it is regarding my client. In your testimony before this Tribunal, you testified that you saw my client on two occasions: On the 18th, and you have his first and last name in your notes; and on the 20th when you recognised him at the bridge during his conversation with Mr. Bosinger, and I presume later on at the hospital, but we will discuss that later as well. In any case, you saw Sljivancanin on the 18th and the 20th. And I believe it is not in dispute, and I believe Mr. Moore will be glad to hear that Mr. Sljivancanin noted his name in your notes himself; therefore, your meeting at Negoslavci is not in dispute. But I'm interested in the following: You told my learned friend, Mr. Vasic, that during your missions you met a lot of people, and you mentioned that there over 100 officers and that is the reason why you can -- you cannot remember everyone, but you can clearly remember what my client looked like, and you remember his name, and as you said that in the Dokmanovic case, am I wrong if I infer that the fact that you remembered his name and face, because he appeared a lot in the media; in particular, his conversation at the bridge with Mr. Bosinger because it was broadcast so often at the time and subsequently? Is that the reason why you remembered him so clearly, or is there something else because of which you remembered him in particular?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a strange analytic memory, and I don't remember so much faces, but I do remember my feelings from -- from this meeting, and what I was surprised of, and probably it's the reason why I do remember that, why I remember Major Sljivancanin, is not only that I saw him on -- on TV, but from this meeting I remember his behaviour, his style of speaking. And I was surprised, because there were even some colonels sometimes, and comparing if there are in a normal army, if there is somebody with a rank two -- of two ranks higher, then those -- this chain of command or superiority is -- is -- is usual by ranks. It's army. And what I remember is that he behaves, he behaved himself like body with -- with certain very high capacity. It could be because he is trained for -- for some PR or -- I can't say, but it is visible that he sometimes overshadowed even higher rank officers. So maybe it is the reason why I am remembering him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I presume that you remember that there were always journalists around him at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him in front of houses speaking to TV cameras and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether any senior officer stood up or confronted him as regards his statements?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you under an impression that he was to be the person to contact journalists on behalf of the JNA during the period when you were there?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it was only because of journalists. He was very visible, and I was thinking what is behind the scene, because sometimes it happens in those type of armies that if there are some special context or some special tasks, so then even lower rank officers are in reality working as a higher officer. So as I -- as I do remember the situation there, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We will go back to the events at which he was present later on. But could we please put Exhibit 303 before the witness? For you that is tab 3 in the folder. It's a sketch showing the structure of your mission. You discussed this with the Prosecutor already, the Prosecutor of -- of the Belgrade HQ of your mission?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You testified, as far as I understood, that as of September 1991 you were appointed as deputy head of the mission, Ambassador Perrin?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The answer was: "Yes, it is correct"? Can you tell me when was this drawn up? In the explanations, I see that November is mentioned and that certain people were on vacation. Can you remember to what period this refers to?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I don't see Mr. Schou anywhere. Can you remember when he joined your mission in relation to the Vukovar events?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of changing and -- of those monitors, and I was many times on the spot, so I don't -- I really had no complete evidence about each and every monitor all the time. I do remember Dr. Schou being on those meetings in Negoslavci before 18th and 19th. Or not -- not before the 18th and 19th, but -- but on those meetings, at least at one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where would his position be within this diagram? So if we take a look at the abbreviations, where would he be placed on the 18th and onwards in relation to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... he was in one of ordinary monitors, but sometimes we made, if it is necessary, so we made a special team consists of -- of few persons which have a special capacity. So it is not -- the teams are stable, but not all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, you, as deputy head of the mission, were his superior in terms of hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the hierarchy, yes. If you ask me on the -- what was on the spot, then it's another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, and in your answers to Ms. Tapuskovic's questions and on several other occasions, you testified as to your duties at the time within the mission, and you told us that your reports were forwarded to the headquarters of the mission in Zagreb. Where did those reports go further? To any central focal point, or whether they were being distributed to those who needed to see them?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an EC, European Community Monitoring Mission. In the time republic was not a member of European community, so I cannot say about the system officially from -- from the sight of Czech Republic, and I don't know, and I didn't know in that time what is the procedure of -- of analysing of those reports, comparing, asking for some other actions and so on. So I cannot -- I cannot say anything about procedures in Zagreb, because in Zagreb I was a very ordinary monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I heard yesterday what you said about Czechoslovakia's status within the mission. But I want to ask you this: I assume that as a member of the mission and as a diplomat you closely followed public declarations made by the Council of Europe and other European institutions at the time, those statements that were made public in the media. As a citizen, once you learn about a declaration like that by, for example, the Council of Europe, did you at the time see that there was anything in reference to your mission, that the reports of your mission were used when making public political declarations?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I told you, in the mission in Belgrade I was really exhausted because of my many functions. So even when I was following press, radio and so on, I was trying to pick up a very concrete situation from the spot or from the society. The level of conferences, Council of Europe and so on, it belongs to the top of the mission in Zagreb, and it was not -- I had no, really, capacity to cover everything, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just let me say something about my question. Page 22, line 10, I referred to the Council of Europe and the OSCE, and this was not recorded in the transcript. What about your reports, I mean you from Belgrade? Were these available to the public? For example --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those reports are only for the tasking cell Zagreb, and it's up to them what they will publish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You must -- I have to be able to finish my answer [sic] because my answers are not recorded in their entirety. I said in my answer [sic] on page 22, line 21, I said: For example, the media in Serbia. And your answer was recorded.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My answer was that our reports were for mission sense to tasking cell to Zagreb, and it was on Zagreb's headquarters what they will publish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the first day of your testimony you described the mission's remit, and you said that the name itself implied what the mission's remit was. It was mainly about monitoring; it wasn't about being involved in negotiations. You even went on to describe how in Ilok you were in other rooms too. Despite which, on the first day of your testimony on page 81, officially the page number is 6562, when you were asked by the Prosecutor about your notes and how you compiled them, you said: "[Previous translation continues] [In English] ... negotiating or referring to this at this point afterwards." [Interpretation] You described the reports, you described Colonel Cunningham, and in the same sentence you say that you two were involved in negotiations. "[In English] -- referring to this and at that point afterwards." [Interpretation] I am just extracting that phrase. But what I want to know is whether you were actively involved in any negotiations. When I say "negotiations," I mean purely the grammatical sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, speaking about negotiations means that, for instance, the evacuation of the hospital. So there are few parties, International Red Cross, we, JNA, and we were negotiating concrete step. Otherwise we were sometimes as witnesses or as a part which -- which facilitating the possibility of contacts of those two sides and we were sitting there as well. Maybe there could be some other mandate, but I don't remember. It depends on situation, because if both sides are agreed, then we can do even more, probably, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, on page 24, line 1, you said, and this wasn't recorded, you said -- you said: "[In English] -- people, evacuation of the hospital." [Interpretation] You said evacuation of the hospital. Didn't you say that a while ago?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the audio recording, so ... Okay. Let's move on to Exhibit 312; this is at tab 17. You've testified about this already, especially what you explained to Mr. Vasic yesterday. Based on that, my understanding was that this is a report -- or should I call it a document, although it does say report 138 of the monitoring mission. So that this was a report made by a special group in order to look into some complaints made by certain authorities regarding breaches of protocol. So it was a special group that drafted this report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness said, "I believe so."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I -- I don't remember consistency of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on this document, sir, can you say anything about the procedure itself. If this was sent from Zagreb, who would have produced a document like this, if you can give me the person's name or the person's position within the mission?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I look at the document, I see that this is dated the 8th of November. And there is a report on breaches of protocol. For example, there is one dated the 7th of November, 1991. What follows, the text that follows, is that, according to you, the report made by the head of mission?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you can look at the top of the page, it says: "Reference" and then it says: "Next report."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The reference "HOM" on the 7th of November. HOM is, I suppose, head of mission, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was used like head of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person who was head of mission in Zagreb at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know what the composition was of those teams, the teams working on the ground gathering information. You said they had lawyers, you said they had other experts on their teams and so on and so forth. You don't know who was doing the cross-checking, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the constituents of the team. And who was doing what.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My understanding was you made a photocopy of this document and gave it to the OTP. I suppose you found it in the archive of the mission, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you made a copy of this document and when you gave it to the OTP, do you remember if there were any attachments to it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, and in the text there is "End of text," and no -- I can't say any referring to annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience, sir, when the Zagreb mission sends a report in relation to certain facts, especially when invoking certain witness interviews, would it be normal to attach to any such reports other materials such as photographs or statements, other reports? Do you have any experience yourself to indicate that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I told you that I have no information about procedures of the headquarters in ECMM Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you only found this document in the mission that you forwarded to the OTP in relation to this piece of paper, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this copy was in Belgrade centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be good to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We'll have the first break now and resume at 10 to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me dwell on this document for a while. The report says that an interview was conducted under A with ECMM members of RCC Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there is no "with each member." There is -- there are interviews with ECMM members of RCC Belgrade, not with each member.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are entirely right. That is what the original says. My official translation says "with each member." That's the copy that I was using. Do you remember conducting any interviews with any members of the special team?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I don't remember, and I am not quite sure if, because of the lack of time I was not in a -- in a contact with them, or the -- the discussion was short. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's in the report. Everything about their difficulties while compiling this report. Do you know that anyone from your Belgrade regional centre took part in the drafting of this document? Did anyone tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is on page 1, heading with the numbers, the last sentence of the paragraph is: "[In English] This view was also supported by a written report from the other area." [Interpretation] Do you have any knowledge to indicate that there was a report from another area? If so, do you know from which area?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said before, I had no any information about the work of the team and about resources, witnesses they have met and so on. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll move on to something completely different now. We're done with this document. Let us now move on to what happened on the 18th, 19th and 20th in Vukovar. I will mostly be referring to documents that have already been admitted. I will not be tendering any new documents, but we will look at certain recordings. Please keep your notebook handy, sir. I will now refer to things in your notebook that you also testified in chief about. I will request some clarifications. Based on your testimony and on your notebook, on the 18th of November first you had that meeting in Belgrade, and then you spent over an hour waiting at a check-point I will say in Adasevci [phoen] before you were allowed to enter the Vukovar area. Do you remember, upon leaving Belgrade, that you were being accompanied by a JNA liaison officers? I'm talking about the 18th of November only.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Sometimes we have met them on the road, there was some point of contact, sometimes they went with us from the hotel. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You read out a portion of your own note where you recorded your meeting with Vesna Bosanac at 12.15. The page in your notebook, the last three digits, 761. I would like to remind you that on that day, after Negoslavci, you drove off to Vukovar and later went to Velepromet. My client took you to an elevation called Milovo hill, from which you could see the town. And you could hear that there was still some fighting going on on the 18th of November. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I know that we were there in the neighbourhood, I cannot say when and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the following document now. You were shown this by my learned friend, Mr. Moore. This is at tab 23. The report on the visit of the 18th. Page 2, it reads, third passage in English: "[In English] We visited the town under JNA protection. There was no cease-fire." [Interpretation] The word "no" is underlined. "[In English] Shelling and firing was going on." [Interpretation] Does this perhaps jog your memory about hearing any shelling and firing on that day?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, really, I can't remember, because shooting was there all the time, and it's -- it's really difficult to remember when.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. I will now remind you of your statement to the OTP, the one you gave back in 1996 when your memory must have been a lot fresher. It's page 7 of the statement. Do you have that in front of you, sir? Page 7, paragraph 1, I'm reading the last portion in the brackets. After the fact that you described the fact that you spoke to Vesna Bosanac on the phone, you appear to be saying to the OTP: "[In English] We were instructed by the JNA liaison officer that ECM Mission would not be permitted further telephone contact with the hospital in Vukovar." [Interpretation] You stated that in 1996 to the OTP. Do you remember whether the --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I cannot precisely say what means after, if it was immediately after the -- the phone call or few hours later. I cannot say. But I -- I know that there was some ban on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. At the beginning of your answer, which wasn't recorded, you said, "Yes," page 29.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, my theory is, and I believe there are documents to show this, that the Zagreb agreement, or Raseta's agreement, if you like, was concluded on the 18th of November in the late evening hours in Zagreb. You said that first you received an oral report about this, about the agreement, and it wasn't until later that a copy of it was faxed to you. Can you tell me exactly when you were told about this or familiarised with the details of the agreement and when you received it in writing that may be recorded on the face of the document itself, and it may have been earlier on. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, and I am sure that it was Colonel Cunningham who first mentioned this -- this agreement because I was not aware about this situation. Maybe even -- even the information came from negotiations, because ECMM was a part of those negotiations, as I am aware of. I don't know in what capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you received this report orally from your office in Zagreb, or from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness said, "I believe so." Again, it wasn't recorded. And what I meant was you, as a team, not you personally, sir. At any rate, as for your discussion with Mrs. Bosanac at 1215 hours on the 18th, you did not know about the agreement at that point in time because it had not yet been signed, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This indicates that Vesna Bosanac told you on that occasion that the Red Cross weren't able to make it because there was firing from the right-hand river-bank of the Danube. This is something you wrote down. On that day, or the next day, or the next days, did you receive any information, and I mean above all the ICRC, to indicate that on the 18th, on the morning of the 18th or the afternoon of the 18th, Mr. Borsinger, on behalf of the International Committee of the Red Cross, attended a surrender of a large number of Croatian troops at Mitnica, over 180 Croatian troops, on the 18th, and we've heard a lot of evidence to that effect, surrendered. And the surrender lasted for nearly the whole day.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Well, there's something I need to clarify about the transcript. The first day during your testimony in chief on page 6566, you testified as follows, and if you could look at your diary, your notes, 1225 hours, you stated: "We have requested approval from Zagreb." That's what your note appears to be indicating. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm reading the transcript from two days ago, the 24th. Question by the OTP: "[In English] And what is the next entry, please, is there a timing at 1225?" "Yes. We ask for permission in Zagreb to go there to Vukovar because -- to Vukovar Hospital." [Interpretation] That was your answer. Let me ask you: Do you now remember requesting approval from Zagreb to go to the hospital, or did you request approval from Zagreb for something else? Because there no reference to the hospital in your diary, in your notes?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no other reason to -- to -- to go -- or to ask for permission in Zagreb. It was -- it's immediately connected, so I -- I believe that my memory is -- is right, that it is connected to -- with the visit in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine. That morning you met General Maksimovic in Belgrade; that much is clear. At that time, or later on while you were travelling, and when you were in touch with the liaison officer, so before Vesna Bosanac told you this, did you ever mention that you wanted to go to the hospital to anyone? Did you express this wish to anyone? Did you write down anything about the fact that you didn't go to the hospital in any of your reports?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you now remember that the liaison officer, or my client, Major Sljivancanin, whom you met that day, told you about the fact that on the 18th there was still fighting in the area surrounding the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to jog your memory, and later on we will see the interview at Pavkovic's on the 19th and you being informed that the hospital was under JNA control on the 19th, but if you don't remember, that's all right. Let's move on. Not even the indictment indicates that the JNA was there on the 18th, but I thought maybe you might remember some details. In relation to Exhibit 314, and the fact that my client's first and last names were recorded in your notebook, it seems beyond dispute that he himself put his signature there. Did it ever happen that you handed your notebook to someone so they could sign the notebook?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the position of the ECMM when talking to any of those involved? I mean involved in the clashes, involved in negotiations. Was it the position that there should be no journalists attending these meetings? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we preferred to -- to do that. But it's up to the -- let's say, the -- those parts we are speaking with, if they insist of it, we cannot -- we cannot send anybody out, because it's the responsibility of receiving part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the 18th when you spoke to the JNA? You proposed that journalists be told to leave the room, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the night between the 18th and the 19th, your first visit? I have already heard some answers but I wish to have this clarified. The -- what about the night between the 19th and the 20th, did you spend any of those two nights at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I believe that I slept in Belgrade, but really ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what you said. I can see that you came at 6.45 on the 20th, pretty early. Does this refresh your memory that you may have left Belgrade very early that morning, because one usually remembers such small towns and where you spent the night, I presume?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we, many times, went from the hotel almost in the night, in the early morning, so I -- I cannot say. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As regards that conversation and you meeting my client on the 18th, I believe Colonel Memisevic was there as well, who often wore an olive-drab uniform. Would you say that the JNA liaison officer was present when you met Sljivancanin on the 18th as well?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- sorry. It was usual that those liaison officers were there. I cannot confirm that exactly in that time it -- it has been Colonel Memisevic. And I do remember that sometimes he wore civil clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, do you remember whether your team at any time contacted representatives of the ICRC at Vukovar? Do you remember having seen them that day, and in Negoslavci as well?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at your notes as regards your visit to Velepromet? That's page 6765. Velepromet. The ERN number I mentioned refers to the notes, and that's not exactly the page number. That's not what I had in mind. Your visit was at 2.45 p.m., you entered Velepromet refugee centre, capacity approximately 300 at the most. After that you wrote a sentence in English. Would you be so kind as to read it, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean -- there is a line, so you mean the sentence up or down from Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Up.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. "We stopped all actions now," do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "2.45 p.m., Velepromet." What follows next?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Centrum for refugees, capacity approximately not more than 300, by their own wishes. Adopted a girl." That's one of remarks. And then there is: "Stojanovic Ljubinko, chief of centrum."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it is written, Stojanovic Ljubinko is written by not my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had explained that on the first day. Your entries, they obviously meant something to you at the time. What does it mean what he you said according to their wish? "[In English] By their own wishes."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember what was that in relation to?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that -- that the capacity is such and such, and that people are there by their own wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the report we can see that you spent a quarter of an hour with the prison warden, Stojanovic Ljubinko, that is in tab 23. We have the schedule of the visit there, and -- and you spent some 45 minutes talking to the refugees. Do you remember whether you asked Ljubinko Stojanovic to have the lists prepared for your next visit, the lists of refugees who were there?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that from the spot, but what I remember is that it is written in some of those reports I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to the 19th. That's tab 21, and we've shown quite some interest in the document before. Could we please have the B/C/S version? [In English] Exhibit 316. [Interpretation] I will not try to repeat the questions posed by the Prosecutor or my learned friends. But as you said, this report was compiled by Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... written by Cunningham's hand, but -- but the -- the first part, or not the first part, but there is a part on the first page which is written by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The title reads: "Subject: Negotiations on the evacuation of the wounded." When Mr. Moore was putting questions to you, he used the word "briefing" in relation to this meeting. I term this negotiations. Would you agree with me that you and Colonel Cunningham in your conversation with Pavkovic and others, you stated your position as regards the evacuation from the hospital. It wasn't a pure exchange of information between you and the JNA, but rather expressing your position to let it known to the JNA. That's how I understood your answer.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Cunningham made a reaction, what he heard -- has heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You read out yesterday who participated in the conversation, and you've corrected what needed to be corrected. Paragraph 5 of the fax message that we mentioned rather often. I will not read out the whole thing, but under D, I wanted to focus on one thing only.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the paper you are speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm still with the document you have before you. We will not talk about the fax message, but about the document itself. At d?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can read it out in English. "[In English] Signed by Croat and JNA." [Interpretation] Could you please read that out?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authorities evoked much discussion -- sorry, probably I have to -- so I will read it once more. "Paragraph 5 of fax signed by Croats and JNA authorities evoked much discussion. Colonel Pavkovic stated that prisoners of war would not be allowed to depart, as first the prisoners of war are under JNA control. Second, if he did, Serb irregulars/local citizens would attack the convoy. Third, the pris -- those prisoners of war would be exchanged for JNA prisoners of war at some future time."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since the Chamber has the document as well, could you please read out item g?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "g: The doctors and nurses of old management would be allowed to move where they wishes."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please stay with the document, and take your notes referring to the 19th. Page, three last digits, 769. Could you please read out the entry at 4.15 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is missing the rest of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out from your notes concerning the same meeting the entry you made at 4.15, what is it that you stated?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it is not what I recognised. It is what I wrote down. Not -- it's not my consultation, it's what I wrote down. So: "Serbs, Territorial Defence/volunteers will not allow convoy pass through if there is a single Croatian soldier in it. If the people knew that Ustashas were in" -- original there is "are," but it is a question of grammar -- "they would liquidate you, you and us in the convoy."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't need to read any further. You've read that out already before. But I'm interested in the following: What you stated in your notes as regards 4.35 p.m., it completely tallies with the information provided by Cunningham in the document, in the report that is that you have read out a minute ago. That Pavkovic stated that he wouldn't allow POWs to leave because, the second reason, should he do that, the convoy would be attacked by the Serb irregulars and locals. The conclusion made by Cunningham is basically the same to what you have read out from your notes?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to the same point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you discussed your notes with your -- with Mr. Moore you said that you don't know who stated that, but I wanted to show you what Cunningham said concerning that. And I believe, and you will probably agree with me, that this is in relation to what Mr. Pavkovic had said.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: According the report, yes. I don't remember real situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want you to speculate, but rather I wanted you to compare the documents. To return to your testimony yesterday, actually I'm not certain whether that was yesterday, but when you discussed how team reports were drafted, you said that all of your colleagues kept their own notes and that you compare them and drafted the report. Was that the method used in compiling a report, indeed?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not all -- each time. Sometimes it -- it was done from memory, sometimes -- it depends on -- on the situation on the -- on the spot and what we saw and sometimes it -- reports were very short because there was nothing to report, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To stay with the meeting on the 19th at Mr. Pavkovic's office in Negoslavci, do you remember, first of all, that at some point you were joined by Nicholas Borsinger, the ICRC representative at the meeting, and he left quite shortly afterwards, and Cunningham told him a few things, and then he left? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that the representative of ICRC was there in the 18th or in the 19th. I don't remember any arguments or -- or any conflict between Cunningham and Borsinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you remember what my client looked like quite well. According to the notes about this meeting, my client wasn't present there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I can't say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I presume that had he been present at the meeting you would have entered that in your notes, would you not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not necessary. Those remarks are not a full record of -- of situation. Sometimes we rely on memory, sometimes I rely that somebody else is writing it down, sometimes you don't know who is even coming to the room, because you are in -- in the situation, you are speaking, or you are listening. So I -- it's -- it's difficult, and I -- I have said in the very beginning using my remarks, that it is not a full record of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I presume that would you agree with me that in your notes pertaining to the 19th, you didn't state having seen my client; and in Cunningham's reports for the 19th there is no mention of my client either. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I wanted to read out to you a portion of the transcript for the 27th of March. Your testimony on the 27th of March, Transcript page 6620, I don't believe you have that with you. This was your testimony two days ago. That was during examination-in-chief by Mr. Moore. Regarding ICRC presence, you replied the following: "[In English] I remember that he was objecting that, that he was not allowed to go to the hospital in the evening." [Interpretation] It hasn't been entered into the transcript correctly. "[In English] I remember he was objecting that, that he was not allowed to go to the hospital in the evening." Then Mr. Moore asked you: "[In English] Do you remember if there was any explanation by the JNA why he was not allowed to go in the evening?" [Interpretation] Your reply was -- you said that a couple of days ago. I wanted to ask you the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it seems to be a recurring problem with regard to the transcript. I am not getting answers, or I don't know exactly what the -- what is being said. For example, the answer was: "No, sorry," but that doesn't show on the transcript. And I also know that a lot of the replies are not being recorded. I hope that nothing will ever turn on it, but there must be some problem, I would have thought with regard to the microphone, or the microphone system with the new -- with the new technology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the problem is much more simple, that the next speaker speaks before the previous answers are recorded, or the previous statement is recorded. So we get only one and not both speakers. I have attempted many times to have that corrected. When I think an answer is particularly important, I intervene to ensure that it is. But I must leave it with counsel. If they want the question and the answer, you just have to ensure that you slow down enough for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, could the witness just be reminded what his reply was, please? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said, "No, sorry," as I've read out. And I want to share something with you that we were told by the interpreters. There is an additional problem when we speak in B/C/S and then we immediately switch to an English text, that is a problem in its own, and we should make a short break there as well for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, regarding your reply to Mr. Moore, do you remember that Mr. Borsinger when he saw you as a team on the 20th, did he tell you that he was at the hospital on the 19th and that he left the hospital by himself, although Dr. Bosanac insisted that he stay overnight? This thing that I stated, does it sound familiar to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether on that day you were told by Mr. Borsinger that he received all the lists of those wounded and sick from Dr. Bosanac and that he had those lists with him on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. What I do believe is that I -- I don't remember even any contact of my person and Mr. Borsinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Cunningham, did he have any contact on the 20th with Mr. Borsinger or Mr. Schou, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I can't say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the Chamber, I have been meaning to show the witness, and Mr. Moore too, Mrs. Bosanac's testimony on 686 and 687. We heard that before, so I just wanted to ask if Mr. Borsinger maybe shared this with you, but that's all right, I suppose, we can move on now. Were you a member of the team that visited Vesna Bosanac at the Sremska Mitrovica prison? A report or a document was drafted on that occasion that has been admitted here.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was established during the interview with Mrs. Bosanac that she stated to you and your representatives that on the 19th the JNA arrived at the hospital with two people from the ICRC. That's what the document says. Do you remember any of your colleagues mentioning this insofar as you talked about this at all?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what I know, I know only from this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did any of your colleagues tell you, or did you yourself hear from Borsinger that he told you you said you were not in touch with him. Did any of your colleagues tell you that Borsinger told them that he was not able to enter the hospital on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Maybe it is in some report -- of reports, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you all these things because of what you told Mr. Moore. So you cannot claim that you heard from anybody that Mr. Borsinger had said that he had lodged a complaint because he wasn't allowed to enter the hospital on the 19th, and because of this you don't know what, if any, JNA reaction that was or any complaints that he made. You told that to Mr. Moore, and now you're telling me that you personally don't remember. I'm asking you about your personal testimony. Perhaps the question was a little complicated.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's very simple, really. You said to Mr. Moore what I have just read out. Now I'm asking you: Did you personally hear from Borsinger or from anybody else personally that Borsinger at that point in time said that he had been ejected, or, rather, that he was not allowed to enter the hospital on the 19th, as you said, and that he told the JNA about this in order to complain about it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have it in my memory somewhere, but I cannot say what is the source of this information now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let's move on. Let's go now to the 20th of November. We need Exhibit 320; tab 32 [as interpreted] for you, sir. It's a report that you drafted. You have testified a great deal about this report, about the time-line, about the facts, about the persons that you mentioned between 1 and 6. I will tell you right away what my position is. You state here in relation to a portion where you say a conflict between 1 and 6, that this is really a clash between Sljivancanin and Borsinger, although, in keeping with your report, under 1, you marked Pavkovic. I will now tell you that you were not wrong in your report. My theory is as follows: Mr. Kypr, it is certain that there was a dialogue between Borsinger and Sljivancanin at the bridge. You saw that; you testified about that. What I wish to tell you now is that you were quite right in your report when you say that there was a clash between Pavkovic and Borsinger and that this clash preceded what we watched yesterday. In the same place before Sljivancanin talked to Borsinger there had been a conversation between Pavkovic and Borsinger. We will now analyse this document, and I think I will refresh your memory after all and that the answer will not be, "I don't know." Let's give it a try. This is how it goes: First the document, please, your report. According to this report, you arrived at the Negoslavci headquarters at about 6.45. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the next page, or rather -- yes, on the next page, you enumerate a number of persons from 1 to 6, persons mentioned in your report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could just intervene for the record, this is tab 22, not 32. Carry on, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
