utterances.text: Alongside these persons mentioned in what I will call the introduction in relation to the 20th, you arrived at the headquarters in Negoslavci, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the place is Negoslavci, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say a short briefing with 1, and you have explained that. You explained that this is a reference to Colonel Pavkovic. Well, now I will again have to read, or perhaps you could. This is your handwriting. What is stated under A? If you can, please, read that out for us, sir, or do you want me to read it, if you have a problem with that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I will try. "A) briefing by 1: Some streets are still mined, we must wait. The organisation of convoy is JNA duty, JNA has enough transport means. 'ECMM can only monitor, any objections after.'" The third point is: "The wounded members of 'Croatian paramilitary forces' must stay here (we have been told later by patients that they have been captured and left the hospital before our arrival), as well as some people of former personnel - Dr. Bosanac," and so on. "ECMM team insisted that all wounded and all people and ill people as medical crew should be transported (by the agreement), and that all prisoners of war must be treated by Geneva Convention. ICRC should provide and check the list of all people in hospital and in convoy."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You probably know this document by heart, you've read it so many times, but let's leave it aside for the time being. Can you now please look at Exhibit 333? Can we please put page 1 in B/C/S on the ELMO? This is tab 27 for you. This is a report by Mr. Cunningham in relation to the same day and the same events. It's been admitted. Can I please ask you to read out the first paragraph? If no, I could do that for you.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to me, so if you would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read the B/C/S. I think the acronyms are good, and you can tell me if they aren't. "On arrival at Colonel Pavkovic's HQ in Negoslavci, the contentious points discussed the previous day were again addressed."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, it is not on -- on the return, but on arrival in the original. "On arrival at Colonel Pavkovic headquarters."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll continue in English. I hope we have the B/C/S on our screens so we can follow. "[In English] Colonel Pavkovic remained firm that not all wounded would be evacuated. As a result of direction from General Raseta, Croat paramilitary wounded would have to remain as prisoners of war. He was informed that the Geneva Convention must be applied. Colonel Pavkovic also advised that the JNA had cleared the roads in their sector of all mines. However, due to some damage in localised areas, the convoy would have to bypass these spots. The convoy departed for Vukovar approximately 8.45 hours. The convoy was delayed approximately two hours in the centre of Vukovar in order that the last mines could be cleared on the route to the hospital." [Interpretation] You saw your own report, you saw Colonel Cunningham's report. You two were there together, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your -- yes, we were there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Colonel Pavkovic is clearly mentioned here as the person who provided Mr. Cunningham with information to do with General Raseta's instructions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please now go back to your own notes, the 20th of November. The ERN in your diary is 772 and 773, last three digits. It's what you mentioned to Mr. Moore. You read this out, and I will -- or actually you might, because the first part of your portion on page 773 and it begins with "the wounded members." If you can, please, sir, read that out for us.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The wounded men of paramilitary" -- sorry, I have to wait -- "of paramilitary formations should stay here. That's definitely a solution with General Raseta."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, can we agree that what you established in this note is quite consistent, if not identical to what Mr. Cunningham wrote in paragraph 1 on his report which you've just read? Meaning that Pavkovic said that not all of the wounded would be evacuated as a result of instructions from General Raseta; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Moore asked you about this particular portion of your notes, you didn't know who said this. But now you've read Cunningham 's report, and you now know that you wrote on the previous page that on the 20th you were with Colonel Pavkovic. You will agree that it's a distinct possibility that Colonel Pavkovic said this and this was recorded by Mr. Cunningham, what you wrote in your own notes?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those two texts refers to the same point. But in my remarks I -- I have no evidence who -- who was the -- the speaker, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we look at this, and I'm not going to read it, because you read entire parts of your diary to the Prosecutor and all I can notice is that it's perfectly consistent with this portion, but we'll move on to something else now, to a different topic. So let's not dwell on this now. Let us now talk about the incident at the bridge. I'm trying to take a chronological approach here in terms of your report and other documents. In your report you said that -- well, shall we say in the centre of Vukovar, and that should be near the bridge over the Vuka River, that you waited there until 10.45. That's what your report says, right? And as far as I remember, you testified -- you know which document I'm talking about, right, that you were -- you testified that you were, together with Mr. Schou and Cunningham, near the place where the dialogue between Sljivancanin and Borsinger took place, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, this is what your report says. I will read it out to you. This is under C, paragraph 2. What it reads, that's what I'm reading, what it says. "The clash between 1 and a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross, number 6, who asked to assume full responsibility of the hospital (they weren't allowed) the JNA requested from the ICRC their written consent to assume full responsibility of the hospital." During your testimony you said that although 1 means Pavkovic in your report, the actual clash occurred between Sljivancanin and Borsinger. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember now. But, sir, there is a mistake in translation. In my remarks there is, "They claimed written agreement," and you have said "saglasnost," which means [indiscernible], so permission or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. What I am using is an official translation, but only your original document constitutes evidence. So I don't think the Chamber will have any problem with this. If you can please now again look at Mr. Cunningham's report about the same thing. What I'm about to read is a somewhat longish paragraph. I think it's really essential that we clarify a number of points of here. This is page 430, the last three digits, paragraph 7. The heading is "ICRC leader behaviour-Vukovar evacuation." "[In English] The ICRC representative first came to my attention in the town of Negoslavci when I observed he and Colonel M, our JNA liaison officer, having a heated argument about something. Some hours later the ICRC representative unexpectedly joined my meeting with Colonel Pavkovic. Purpose of the meeting was to resolve all points in the fax message regarding the Vukovar Hospital evacuation. I explained that he was responsible to action paragraph 6 of the fax and also responsible to make and keep detailed lists of all persons leaving the hospital. He departed the meeting with no explanation." [Interpretation] Can we now please focus on this portion, and I will ask you about the previous portion. "[In English] The next time I saw him was in the middle of Vukovar having a loud verbal shouting match/disagreement with Colonel Pavkovic. Not wishing to be involved, the other two monitors and I retired to our vehicle. I learned later that the argument centred on the fact that the Vukovar Hospital was under the protection of the ICRC with all the associated implications. Colonel Pavkovic stated that he had not been informed and therefore he was proceeding with his plans. I contacted Z to attempt to obtain some info. However, contact" -- I think it's -- "contact was poor, and I did not receive the entire message. Shortly after the ICRC representative approached my vehicle and demanded in an abrasive manner to talk about the neutrality issues. I informed him that I did not have all the facts and would only discuss the issue when I had. I remind him of his responsibilities" -- I don't know what's the meaning of "PD" -- "of neutrality and lists."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Period, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Which he ask as having been told." Something is wrong. "He departed in an agitated manner." [Interpretation] Another brief portion: "[In English] After a wait of some 1.30 hours, the convoy departed to the hospital where upon the ICRC stormed into the" -- I don't know the meaning of "grds"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And in the previous paragraph "ack," acknowledged rather than asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "And I lost sight of him." [Interpretation] Just to have this in a proper context, I will finish this. "[In English] Next saw him in his vehicle shouting into a microphone. At the request of STO, I asked if he had any control over the proceeding. He replied no in a derogatory voice and answered that he was going to hold a press conference to announce to the world what was happening in Vukovar." [Interpretation] First and foremost, this document authored by Mr. Cunningham is what you provided to the OTP; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, they are not on my copy. Yes, on -- on the page 1428 I can see that, but not in -- on previous pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In -- could I comment for the record that in the numbering, two pages appear to be in reverse order. One, the numbering 00331430 should come before 1429; and the handwritten numbering at the top right-hand of 1 out of 3, 2 out of 3, 3 out of 3, pages 2 and 3 should be reversed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tapuskovic is looking at me, and I can tell you that all three teams spent considerable time putting those documents together, and I believe the OTP must have too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, a few things to ask first, because I believe this portion of the document merits our attention. Do you remember having seen on the first day, or perhaps not the first day, but did you see Borsinger in a confrontation with Colonel Memisevic? Perhaps you saw them having an argument?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In one of your replies a minute ago, you said that you think he joined one of the meetings. Colonel Cunningham mentions it was the 19th at Pavkovic's office. Does this refresh your memory that Borsinger was there at the time and that there was some sort of reaction by Colonel Cunningham? You read out yourself what Mr. Cunningham told him on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any comments made by Cunningham after the meeting as you were going back to Belgrade or the next morning or perhaps by Mr. Schou, according -- that is concerning his entries in the report?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It states clearly here that Cunningham saw Pavkovic and Borsinger had a disagreement in Vukovar. You would agree with me, I believe, that what Mr. Cunningham states tallies with your report where you wrote that there was an -- a confrontation between Pavkovic and Borsinger. That's what your report reads and that tallies with what Mr. Cunningham wrote down? Your report was the document that we read a moment ago. Again, I will remind you to -- I will remind you of my theory. Do you remember that before the confrontation, or dialogue between Borsinger and Sljivancanin there was another argument by Borsinger and Pavkovic, and that's what you entered in your report. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I really have in my memory now is that it was a discussion between Major Sljivancanin and a representative of International Red Cross. And I am really not aware of anything more, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you wrote in your report, that is confrontation between Pavkovic and Borsinger, tallies completely with what Cunningham wrote down?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but still in my memory there is -- sorry. There is Major Sljivancanin as an -- so what is written is written, what I remember is -- is that. So it's what I can say about it. And maybe -- I do remember that even in -- in my first testimony in the previous case I -- I have mentioned maybe even Major Sljivancanin as discussing. So it's what I remember. This is what was visible for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, you testified in the Dokmanovic case, and it is certain that my client spoke with Mr. Borsinger and you testify about that in that case. But in addition to that, I wanted to ask you the following: What you wrote in your report, does that tally with what Mr. Cunningham wrote down? That's all I'm asking. And after the break we will show a recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position is being put, Mr. Lukic, whether there is a mistaken identification between Major Sljivancanin and Colonel Pavkovic. Could it not be that there were two separate incidents? One involving your client and a separate one involving Colonel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will keep the suspense alive after -- until after the break, because we will play a recording, and I believe it will be interesting for all those participating in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry then. I thought that you were putting one issue only, not seeing the other possibility. We will resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just deal with one preliminary matter, and I think the Court may have already notice of it. I think the Ambassador has certain timing difficulties. I for my part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention what we can do? Judge Thelin and I are in a Plenary meeting all afternoon. We can sit through with the tape until 2.15. We cannot sit beyond that. So that if Mr. Lukic can finish in one hour, you can have 25 minutes. Even if Mr. Lukic can do it in 55 minutes, you can have half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm quite sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be near enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Lukic can be done by half past 1.00, and I can have three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will see whether I will able to meet your expectations time-wise. I would kindly ask the usher for the assistance. Let's see Exhibit 318; that is the recording of the conversation at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to remind you that at the beginning of the dialogue Mr. Borsinger says, "The colonel knows what the problem is, ah, there he comes." And we don't need to proceed with the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now go back to the old-fashioned way and -- to look at a portion of the videotape? I forwarded the transcript of the dialogue to the OTP and to the registry. Perhaps that can be provided for the Bench. And the interpreters have that as well. I would like to apologise for a poor recording, but I believe during recertification I will be able to get a hold of a version that is of better quality. We didn't plan to use this this early, but we wanted to have that introduced with Mr. Kypr.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, do you have before you the transcript of what we are about to see?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the witness received his copy. Could we please begin with the recording?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kypr, first of all, did you recognise anyone in the recording?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Borsinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you recognised him as having a conversation with Sljivancanin. Do you recognise Colonel Pavkovic on the recording, because you spoke with him on that very day, and the day before?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise -- I believe you need to repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... No, I don't remember the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the locality or do you recognise anyone else; for example, Colonel Memisevic?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The recording you saw, you don't remember being there before the dialogue between Borsinger and Sljivancanin occurred. But yet you put that in your report to remind you an argument between Pavkovic and Borsinger. One can read that in your report.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do remember is that I saw the discussion -- that I saw the discussion between Major Sljivancanin and Mr. Borsinger. On this footage I saw the place that it is near the bridge or on the bridge, but I cannot say precisely where it is, if it is on -- on which place directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm for me whether you stated in your report that there was an argument between Pavkovic under your number 1, and Borsinger, number 6. Is that what is stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I mark this footage as video one. Could that be tendered as an exhibit? And the transcript, in its electronic version, be marked as 0D05-0318, and I'd like to tender that separately. I again can say that this is the recording I have, and I will try to get a better copy over Easter vacation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Both the video -- oh, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to the video, I have no objection to that being admitted as an exhibit. With regard to the transcript, I don't know if it assists my learned friend, on page 4, second -- the penultimate comment by Nicholas Borsinger, I heard, "Because since I was blocked." Now, I see my learned friend Mr. Lukic agreeing with that. If in actual fact the word is "blocked," and it seems to be it's agreed, then I will agree to the transcript, subject to the Defence -- subject to the Prosecution having, as it were, another look at the transcript itself. But certainly that's the one alteration that was very obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to explain - Mr. Moore reminded me of something - we forwarded this for official translation, and perhaps this can temporarily be marked for identification, and the official translation will be provided for the translation service, and that will be the exhibit then. For the time being, it can be MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The video will be received as an exhibit. The transcript of it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video will be exhibit number 335, while the transcript will be MFI 336.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on, Mr. Kypr, to try to wrap things up. Yesterday you told my learned colleague, Mr. Vasic, you said that you don't remember who told you once you were at the hospital that some patients had been taken away already. I will remind you of your testimony in the Dokmanovic case on the 11th of February, 1998, page 1374. The question by the OTP: "[In English] Did anyone tell you whether or not other patients had already been removed?" Answer: "Yes, we were told both by the patients and by the hospital staff that we met in the hospital. They told us that some of the patients had already been taken away, and also some of the doctors had been taken away." Question: "Did they say which of the patients had been taken away?" Answer: "I don't remember anybody specifying any names." Question: "But did they -- okay." Answer: "As for names, I know that Dr. Bosanac was missing." Question: "No, I'm not after names. I'm asking, were there any particular types of patients or persons that had been removed? Were you informed of that?" Answer: "Yes, we had been told that these are the patients that Yugoslav army had been suspected of being Croatian soldiers." [Interpretation] I presume you remember those events back in 1998 more than you do today. And this is what you stated in 1998, you described the persons who provided information to you.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you entered the hospital after 10.45 you entered together with Mr. Cunningham and Mr. Schou; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't remember the situation when I first time went into the hospital. But I believe so, that we were three.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember discussing the information you received from the patients and the medical staff between the three of you at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember real situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you as members of the team together in the hospital, did you leave the hospital together that day?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that during the whole day I was mostly alone working outside. In few cases I went into the hospital, but I believe that Dr. Schou was mostly inside. We were for lunch to eat our -- to eat our packets of food, so I believe that we were together in that time, but I can't say more. It was a really dramatic situation, so I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of any of the other members of the team telling Mr. Borsinger what they heard, what they were told by the medical staff in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony the other day you said you spent the evening in Sremska Mitrovica. You arrived there on a convoy, and you were there together with Mr. Schou and some other people. My question, therefore, is if you discussed this with the civilians who were there and whether they told you that some of those people had been taken away and some were on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no time to speak with them so much, so I had to inform them about the situation, what will be the next procedure. And there were many places I had to do that, so I don't remember that -- that I have got any of those informations and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yours, Mr. Lukic, won't switch on; mine won't switch off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Either yourself or any of your colleagues, did you ask Mr. Borsinger for the lists of the wounded when you saw him there and when he was giving an interview to the journalists in the hospital that day? Did you ask him whether he had any lists and whether -- and did you ask him to give them to you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you reached the hospital at 10.45, did anyone prevent you from moving about the hospital, to be present when the wounded were being taken in or to list people? Were you prevented to do that by anyone at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you reached the hospital, did you see anyone preventing Nicholas Borsinger to enter the hospital when -- either Mr. Borsinger or some other representatives of the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your diary you wrote - let me just find that - what the ICRC would do. This is page 774, that's the ERN number. You wrote: "The ICRC will check the wounded based on the list at the beginning of the evacuation and after." That's what you wrote. What I'm asking you is: Did you actually see the ICRC, any of their men, do this while you were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked by the Prosecutor about the loading process, the wounded boarding the buses. Can we please now go to tab 27, Exhibit 333? What Mr. Cunningham, your colleague, wrote in that report. I'll be reading the English, just to hurry things along. I'm reading paragraph 2: "[In English] As a result" -- [Interpretation] I'm just reading the bit that's relevant for me. "[In English] Inordinate amount of confusion" --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me, I can't find this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry, I didn't give you the reference. It's paragraph 2. Page 1, paragraph 2, line 4. "[In English] When the hospital evacuation first started, walking wounded, elderly people and children streamed out of the hospital en masse."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, I cannot find it in my text. Can you help me with ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quoting a document that is at tab 27, Mr. Cunningham's report. I'm reading from paragraph 2 on page 1, midway through the paragraph, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you got that now, sir? "[In English] The majority of the old administration instead of helping evacuation the hospital or -- or care for the injured sat in front of the building in the hospital compound doing nothing. Ambulance had some difficulty getting to the hospital door and crowd of extraneous personnel congregated in front of the hospital doors, effectively impeding the orderly movement of the wounded into the waiting ambulances."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "Impeding. Effectively impeding." Preventing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document has already been admitted. We don't need to go on reading this. But, sir, you said you spent most of the time outside in the courtyard and not inside the hospital. Do you remember scenes like these, like the one described by Mr. Cunningham about loading the wounded?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we had problems in the entrance, because people, many people were moving in and out. And I remember a group of -- of people who were standing and sitting near the hospital with very sad faces. It's all what is in my memory as a -- is that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These same facts are also stated in Exhibit 321, the official report compiled by the Zagreb mission, but I'm not dwelling on that now. You have just told me what you remember, and we can take it from there. Can you please now go to tab 20? It's the Zagreb agreement, so to say, Raseta's agreement. [In English] Exhibit 40, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can you please look at paragraph 1 of the agreement indicating who the parties are. It says: "Agreement concerning the evacuation convoy for wounded and patients of the Vukovar Hospital"; is that right? If could you please look at paragraph 4, the second sentence of paragraph 4. "Both parties will provide suitably equipped and manned ambulances for some 40 seriously ill and lorries or coaches, as appropriate, for the remaining 360 or so casualties of whom around a third will be stretcher cases." That's what the agreement states, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there any reference in this agreement to doctors and medical staff? Yes or no, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go through the whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you are about to, what I want to know is about doctors, medical staff, other hospital employees or civilians. What about these three categories? Is there any reference in this document to any of these?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will now remind you what, and this is Exhibit 319, this is Mr. Borsinger's statement that we looked at some days ago, what he stated on that occasion, just to keep us from going back to the transcript, so what I'll do is read a portion out to you. Mr. Borsinger says: "[In English] According to this agreement, access to the hospital and compound in which we are now standing was limited to sick and wounded civilians and military personnel. This is the first category. The second category was civilians who were not participating in the conflict. The third category were medical personnel and administrative staff of the hospital. And the fourth was ICRC delegates. Point three of this agreement was that no weapons would be allowed in the neutralised zone, and any military materials will be removed from the compound." [Interpretation] Does this agreement reflect any of the things specified by Mr. Borsinger, the one you've just gone through?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that as a whole, but I think that no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, what about paragraph 4 of the agreement? There is some reference there to 40 seriously ill persons and about 360 wounded. This is the agreement dated the 18th. Now, your document, your report, that's at tab 22, your report dated the 20th, if you could go to that, please. You establish under d, Vukovar Hospital. Can you follow, sir? "Cellar of the former medical centre and nuclear shelter. Crowded with patients (300 to 400)." You wrote this, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we now please go to tab 34? When Vesna Bosanac spoke to your colleagues at Mitrovica, you weren't present, but this is on page 08 for you, the very first line. "[In English] 392 wounded in hospital." [Interpretation] This is what she stated to your colleagues, and the transcript was based on her statement, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you could now please go to tab 25. Exhibit 321. If we could please have the B/C/S on our screens. The page is 03040387. This is page 3 in the B/C/S, where it says "Belgrade and Sarajevo teams." I believe it's page 3 in English as well. It reads -- this is the official report from your mission in Zagreb, right, this document? This is how it reads: "At 1430 hours the team reported, a, that 82 wounded were loaded on an ambulance; b, that 263 injured persons who were still able to walk boarded the bus; c, the convoy included 17 doctors, 6 nurses, and 11 escort personnel. At this point in time 110 wounded patients remained in the hospital awaiting arrangements for transfer to Belgrade or Novi Sad. A further 52 patients were also in the hospital because of insufficient transport. Plans were made for these to be collected the following day." Is this what your team reported at 1430 hours, as I read in the heading? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. And I doubt that it was my team, because we were in the spot where the communication with our mobile phones was not possible. So I believe that -- or some other team or when we came somewhere on the top, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate, this information was forwarded to your headquarters in Zagreb because they eventually produced this document, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will not be dealing with these documents any further. I think I'm about to wrap it up as far as documents are concerned. There is a portion of your testimony in the Dokmanovic case that triggered my curiosity and you haven't spoken about this. This is page 76 of the transcript, but I think you may be able to remember the relevant portion even without looking at it. Do you remember that when you arrived outside the hospital there was a desk or some sort of a wheelchair or a table with some sharp implements on top of it? You testified about this in the Dokmanovic case. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was that exactly? Will you tell the Chamber, please, about this. What exactly did you see, and where exactly was this? There is a sketch that you drew at the time, and we can show you the sketch for you to refresh your memory. This is -- if we can have this displayed on our screens, please, the diagram. 0D05-0026, if that can be shown, please. This is tab 36 for you, sir, for your reference. It will soon come up on the screen. Please tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the sketch of the hospital in the very centre, and there is a way down to the entrance to the cellar. It is from the right side of the sketch. Number 1, there was a heap of around 100 plus, but maybe less, I didn't count it, of sharp things. Scissors, small knives, Swiss knives, some scalpels, I do remember. And a very similar situation was in number 2. It was a hospital trolley, on which there was a heap of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this sketch admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 337.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you now remember, did you ask any questions about where those implements came from? Did you ask anyone about those implements?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll have to go back to a particular document briefly. This is tab 22, sir. Your report of the 20th. Just a minute, please. As far as I can see, under h) it says that on the 21st of November you and Mr. Schou went to the Negoslavci headquarters, that's what it says. It goes on to say: "Briefing in Negoslavci HQ. Number 2 took 3 buses." Do you remember that time you went to Negoslavci and when you spoke to General Crmaric. Crmaric, Jerko Crmaric?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my text, but I don't remember those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you by any chance remember that on the 21st when, according to this report, you were in Negoslavci Borsinger came over to speak to my client about the problem that had arisen? Does this trigger a memory, does this ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. What I know, that we -- we got a list of patients from ICRC, but it was in the hospital, I believe, not -- not on the meeting. But I cannot guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, I'm about to wrap it up. I'm now reaching my two final conclusions, based on the course of my cross-examination. Please tell me if you agree with these. Based on all these reports and documents that we have been analysing for the last couple of days, in relation to the taking away of patients from the Vukovar Hospital before your arrival, the only reference in your document, in this document, is where you say that a number of patients told you this or that. But you can't find any reference in any of the other documents, the document compiled by Mr. Cunningham or the one compiled by the Zagreb mission. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said so. I don't remember if there is any evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've gone through the documents indicating the number of wounded. I will ask you to please go back to the final part of the conclusion of the Zagreb mission; this is tab 25, Exhibit 321. The figures are there. The conclusion under 11, number 11. Can you please read that conclusion out for us?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The number of sick and wounded handed over and then subsequently delivered to Djakovo are in line with the agreement, e.g., around 400 or so."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My theory, Mr. Kypr, is that the persons who were taken away no doubt before you reached the hospital, were not patients of the Vukovar Hospital, because the number tallies with what had been agreed on the 18th of November and with whatever was indicated in the Zagreb report. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was expecting this sort of an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have hereby concluded my cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the previous answer --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't hear any answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have to pick up the last two answers, Mr. Lukic. I suspect they're important to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May the witness please answer?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would speak now, please, Mr. Kypr.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal, please, with certain topics, and I will try and do it sequentially. You were asked about the -- what I will call the Bapska ultimatum. And if we look at what we now call Exhibit 305, that's tab 6. Would you be kind enough, please, to turn your documents, and I will deal with it, I hope, fairly quickly. Now, you should have in front of you handwritten document starting RCB, is that right, and on the top right-hand corner you've got numbers 1 to 7 or 1/7. Do you see that or not?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, if we can just move two lines down from the top, we can see team 7, 8th of October, 1991. Mission Ilok, see Annex A. Can you just confirm that, please, in a loud voice?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, we can see if we turn over the page we have got 1 of 7, 2, 3, 4, then we have got what seems to be Annex A, but it's -- just carrying on, 5 of 7, which is almost in the top of the middle. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then 6 of 7. And if we turn over, we can see 7 of 7, it was clearly Annex A, but for whatever reasons been made annex C. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So with regard to the question, the Bapska ultimatum, is it right or not that in actual fact that that ultimatum, I will use the word travelled with that particular report or using the numbers? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to my own knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on then, please. You were asked about the overall situation in relation to Bapska and the surrounding area. And you said it was difficult to describe the sort of environment that you were working in. What I want to know, please, is what did you mean by the sort of environment that you were working in when you were asked about that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we saw in one village already burning house, in other villages there were burnt houses. So the situation was very, very sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what about JNA control or military control existing around Ilok and Bapska and those other places that you visited?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told by JNA that there is no JNA in this part of -- of the territory, because they cannot guarantee us safety if they are there, so our safety is -- is fully guaranteed. It's what we were told. What I saw, there were some groups of volunteers, as I described in -- in my remarks about Lovas, and entrance to Lovas, but we saw another group during our way, I believe, near Sarengrad, but I -- I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, can I deal with -- I'll deal with Lovas now, if I may. You were asked various questions by Mrs. Tapuskovic and the drive of the questions seemed to be that there was -- the ICRC had basically not fulfilled the requirements or standards that you would normally require -- my words. Now, could I ask you, please, to look at tab 26? It's our Exhibit 322. And I would like you to look, please, at the page number 00381426. The subheading is "the Belgrade regional centre." Have you got that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with the point how easy it was for the ICRC to do their work. If we deal with paragraph 11, can we start, please, four lines down. With the sentence beginning "however." Would you be kind enough to read that out, please?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "However when the team arrived in Vukovar they found that the JNA were running the operation. The International Red Cross had been ejected from the hospital at 2000 hours on the 19th of November."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's 2000 hours. Can I just then direct you to the transcript, which the Defence, if I can locate it, the Defence have provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If Your Honour will forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This is a document that is marked for identification. Do you have a copy of that transcript of the video that was shown to you by Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to just turn to bottom of the page or bottom corner, page number 4? Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll read it out, makes it easier perhaps. Borsinger's last reply of that day: "Because since I was blocked" -- as I submit that it is. Turn over the page. Borsinger: "No, no, I meant to be." Then going on again. Borsinger: "I meant to be ... according to this agreement I meant to be in the hospital since last night at 8.00." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I just ask you, please, to look at one other document? It is tab 25. That is our Exhibit 321, I believe. And I'll try and find the page. Yes. It's page 1419. It comes under the general heading of Vukovar relief mission, but I would like you to look at page 1419, b, (i), and it relates to the 20th. Now, have you got that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Perhaps if I read it. On the 20th of November, and then it goes on to say about going to Vukovar, may I drop down, then, six lines, just after "drunk and aggressive, dead bodies were visible in the ruins. On arrival at hospital, they found that the JNA were in control and the International Red Cross had not been permitted entry to the hospital to begin the registration of sick and wounded." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. So, when in actual fact Ms. Tapuskovic, or counsel on behalf of Mr. Radic, asked you questions about the ability or capability of the ICRC being able to do their job on the evening of the 19th and indeed the 20th, do you rely on these documents or your own knowledge? Can you assist us? Or a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a combination of both. Because after 15 years, it's difficult to rely only on my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, indeed. You have been asked questions about your evidence in the Dokmanovic case by counsel on behalf of Mr. Radic. And I'd like to deal with a part of that. If I may be allowed just to locate it. Yes, it really relates to the visit to Lovas and the fact you were asked about the military commander. The reference is, I believe, page 10, line 13. And the suggestion was that the gentleman that you considered to be apparently a little unstable, that he had obtained provisions for the village. Do you remember that -- that piece of evidence that was referred to by my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look, please, at the totality of the evidence that you gave in relation to this situation at Lovas. Would it be possible, please, for the registry to be able to turn up that page? It is page number -- as I have it, 1364. I believe you may find it on ERN 1351 through to 1383, but I can't guarantee that. Yes, is there any way that it can be blown up so that people can read it? Because I certainly can't. Can you read it, Mr. Kypr? I know you have problems with your eyesight?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can it be expanded?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, you mean the whole page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for the page to be enlarged because it really -- you need almost a magnifying glass. So page 1364, I think, will be the starting point.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I use my hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If you've got a hard copy, I have no objection. Thank you very much. Have you got a series of hard copies, a number of pages, or just one?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the whole --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we go top right-hand corner, page 1364.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Commander" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I go to line 7.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question was: "Did he say what his position was, if you can recall." Answer: "I think if I remember it correctly, he said he was the military commander and he also said he was -- what would be a mayor." There we are that's much better. Question: "The mayor of the town. Did he say to you why it was necessary that Lovas was attacked?" Answer: "He explained to us that the attack was necessary because in the village there was a Serb minority and they were being threatened by the Croat population. "Did he speak of the need to change the ethnic balance in the town? "If I remember correctly, he did. "Can you tell us, elaborate just a little bit more on that. What did he say? "This was rather surprising, because he was saying that it was essential that the Serb people were moved into the village from the other areas, to change the structure that is unnatural because there was this majority of Croats, but honestly, I do not know whether I remember this correctly because we are talking about a time seven years ago." Now this is the question that I want to deal with, please: "Did he say whether the JNA had played any role in the taking of Lovas? "No, and this again surprised me, because he said that he had invested money and equipment, that he had provided equipment for the unit, that he had liberated the village, that he had invested I cannot remember how many Deutschmarks. I honestly cannot remember how many." Question: "From the observations you made in this region, and having regard to the attacks on the various villages that you witnessed, did you form any view as to the approach that was being taken by the forces on the Serb side in relation to the military tactics of both the JNA, the volunteers and the paramilitaries?" Answer: "What was interesting, perhaps, was that the Yugoslav army rather held positions in the area where these villages were located and there were groups that we referred to as, 'paramilitary groups', at that time." And may I ask, please, to look down at line 25? "What role did the paramilitary groups play, so far as you are able to observe?" Answer: "These were the forces of the first attack, but this is a matter of what we were told, in fact, because in view of the rules under which we operated, we were never in the areas where paramilitary operations were proceeding." I'm sorry to read out such a large part, but I'd like you to look, if you would be kind enough, please, to a document that you've been referred to by both Prosecution and Defence. Would you be kind enough to turn up tab 13? Now, there is reference to Lovas with 26 destroyed houses. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Some were damaged, some very severely." The damage itself, can you remember how the damage had been caused? There's 26 damaged houses.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember pictures I made there, and it reminds me even more, because they were burnt. I -- I can't remember impacts of grenades, of shells, but I remember that they were burnt totally, even -- even garage with tractors and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. So when one deals with the report on tab 17, Exhibit 312, I'd like you to look at page 381382, and you said that you weren't aware if Lovas was used. There is a reference to burning and looting. Does this report and the general conclusion correspond with what you found at Lovas in relation to the burning?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it -- maybe it relates to that, but I don't know if it is the concrete reason for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I deal then with two other topics, I think, and that will be it. There is reference at tab 27, you have been asked about it. It's Exhibit 334, and I want to go to the handwritten version. So it will be page number 00381448. I'm told it's 333, I apologise. Now, can you go to that page number ending 1448? Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't catch the right tab, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. It's my fault, I'm sure. Tab 27.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 27, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It should subdivide into two specific documents. One is typed which has been called Cunningham's report, and then there is a handwritten report.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have only the first page as the handwritten report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got page 1448?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my file it has no those -- there is ZA00-4265, so it's identification at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I can deal with it orally anyway. What is said is that the hospital at Vukovar was visited. And there was a suggestion that from the rooftop planes were shot at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise for interrupting, but it would be fair if we knew what document exactly, and the witness should know as well. Maybe it's document bearing the number of Ky-V-18. It's not amongst the tabs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In actual fact, it's my fault because it is a Defence exhibit which I have put into that tab for relevance. So in actual fact it is a Defence exhibit, I think, and it was given the number 334. I apologise for that. I'm using my own filing system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I will read it out. It's not a problem, I think. The suggestion is that from the rooftop planes were shot at. Now, when you got to Vukovar yourself, and the Vukovar Hospital, did you ever go to the roof personally?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was part of our task to observe the situation, and I believe that I went with Mr. Cunningham, but I cannot guarantee to -- to the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why did you go to the roof?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To observe the situation in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Had there been any suggestion that the roof had been used for weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no such an evidence. We didn't see any traces. Any ammunition there or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for clarification, I think Cunningham is a colonel, or was a colonel, Cunningham, of the Canadian army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then finally this -- it's always dangerous for a barrister to say "finally." Can I deal with the group of people you were told by patients that a group of people had been removed before you had got there from the hospital. In respect of the JNA, did anyone from the JNA inform you that a group had been removed and taken away before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But maybe there is even problem in understanding what was removed, because it can be personnel and Dr. Bosanac, we asked especially for her, so then it's a question of people, which type of people, and I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where did Cunningham go, that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was even in the morning. Or be in the -- soon afternoon. He -- he went to -- to organise the situation and he went to -- to Belgrade ---

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And this is my last question. Did anyone from the JNA ever say to you what I will call the Raseta agreement was cancelled or did not exist?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that concludes the questions that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are very grateful to counsel. And I'm sure the ambassador is grateful as well, because you will be pleased to know that concludes the evidence. We would like to thank you for coming to The Hague, for the assistance you've given us, and despite the strain it's been with your eyes, to try and assist us in these last days. We will now adjourn to resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.09 p.m.,
